div.p: ARINC 653 aims to simplify integration of independently developed (avionics) application software executing on a shared computer platform. A key idea is that the application software is organized as a set of partitions, potentially with different criticality levels, and the underlying operating system attempts to achieve certain isolation properties between the partitions. Unfortunately, when using ARINC 653 on multicore, the existence of undocumented hardware resources makes satisfying real-time requirements challenging. We adapt a previously proposed technique (not for ARINC 653 but for undocumented hardware) so that it works for ARINC 653. The main idea of our solution is to (i) describe the software system as a set of processes and describe each process with parameters, (ii) introduce an abstraction that describes the execution speed of a process as a function of co-runner processes on other processor cores, (iii) empirically find the numeric values of this abstraction, and (iv) use a formal verification technique (called schedulability test) that takes as input the description of processes and outputs a statement on whether all timing requirements will be satisfied at run-time for all scenarios assumed to be possible.

From the perspective of the application software in a partition, the period and duration can be viewed as a guarantee provided by the time-triggered schedule on the supply of processing time. From the perspective of the time-triggered schedule, the period and duration of a partition can be viewed as a requirement on how frequently the partition should receive service and how much. Third, given the period and duration of each partition, one can obtain a function that provides for each possible time interval, a lower bound on the amount of processing time supplied to a partition during this time interval. Fourth, with this lower bound, one can apply techniques that can prove satisfaction of real-time requirements (or disprove it) of a set of concurrent processes given a model of these processes; such techniques are called schedulability analysis or schedulability test in the real-time systems research literature. Unfortunately, with multicore processors, the last activity becomes challenging because of the existence of hardware resources that are shared between processor cores (e.g., cache memory, memory bus); they become even more challenging when the multicore processor has undocumented hardware (i.e., the shared resources within the processor chip and within the memory system are not disclosed by the hardware maker). Therefore, in this paper, we discuss satisfying real-time requirements of multicore software on ARINC 653, specifically the issue of undocumented hardware. To this end, we adapt a previously proposed technique (not for ARINC 653 but for undocumented hardware) [8] so that it works for ARINC 653. The main idea of our solution is to (i) describe the software system as a set of processes and describe each process with parameters, (ii) introduce an abstraction that describes the execution speed of a process as a function of co-runner processes on other processor cores, (iii) empirically find the Fig. 1. ARINC 653 single core numeric values of this abstraction, and (iv) use a formal verification technique (called schedulability test) that takes as input the description of processes and outputs a statement on whether all timing requirements will be satisfied at run-time for all scenarios assumed to be possible. This enables, under certain assumptions, satisfying real-time requirements of multicore software on ARINC 653 even with undocumented hardware. Table I highlights our contribution.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II gives background: understanding how ARINC 653 works on single core; the challenges that multicore brings to satisfaction of timing requirements; how ARINC 653 works on multicore; and our observations on how academics and practitioners have different perspectives. Section III presents model, notation, and terminology that we will use. Section IV shows our new verification procedure (schedulability test). Section V gives conclusions.

div.head: A. Single-core ARINC 653
div.p: ARINC 653 [1,2] is a standard for avionics systems and emphasizes safety. This is a broad scope; in this paper, we focus only on real-time requirements aspects of ARINC 653. Fig. 1 illustrates ARINC 653 for a single-core system. The software system is organized as a set of partitions. The scheduling of the single core is as follows. There is a schedule, called module schedule, whose length is called a major time frame; this schedule is repeated indefinitely. This module schedule contains partition time windows (ptws); a ptw is a time interval characterized by (i) an offset, (ii) a duration, and (iii) the partition that is served during this ptw. In Figure 1, there are four ptws in a major time frame: two ptws serve Partition 1; one ptw serve Partition 2; and one ptw serve Partition 3. A partition is also characterized by its period and its duration meaning that for time intervals of length equal to the period, it holds that the cumulative amount of time that ptws serve this partition in this time interval is greater than or equal to the duration of the partition. The ARINC 653 standard does not mandate a specific major time frame but it states (page 6 in [2]):
The major time frame can be defined by a multiple of the least common multiple of all partition periods in the integrated module. We will not make this assumption; our paper is more general.

A partition may consist of a set of processes. There are two special processes: the main process and the error handling process. The former deals with initialization of a partition and the latter deals with error handling. In this paper, we will ignore them. Instead, we will focus on processes that implement functionality of the application of a partition. Also, in this paper, we focus on the system when it has been initialized (i.e., in case the initialization has real-time requirements, then we ignore that in this paper). In addition, we ignore processing due to error handling in the error process.

In ARINC 653, a process is specified with its period, deadline (called "time capacity" in ARINC 653), whether it is periodic or aperiodic, and whether its deadline is hard or soft. In this paper, we focus only on periodic processes (i.e., we assume that there are no aperiodic processes) and we assume that all processes have hard real-time requirements. We make these assumptions because these are common in the academic literature on real-time scheduling and because these are the type of processes that tend to be safety critical.

A partition has four modes: idle, cold start, warm start, and normal. Idle means the there is no execution in the partition. Cold start and warm start mean that the partition is initializing; they differ only in whether one can assume that main memory needs to be initialized (different power failures may require different types of initializations). Normal mode means that the partition provides normal service; this means that a periodic process needs to satisfy real-time requirements. When a partition switches to normal mode, it waits until time has reached the time when a certain ptw starts; it is a ptw whose attribute periodic processing start is true. Note that a partition may have more than one ptw and a partition may have more than one ptw whose periodic processing start is true. To understand this behavior, consider the example in Fig. 2. It shows a process called Process 6 which is assigned to Partition 1. The period of Process 6 is T6. Let t denote the time when Partition 1 switches to normal mode. Let t' denote the earliest time such that (i) t ≤ t', and (ii) a ptw of Partition 1 starts at time t' and for this ptw it holds that periodic processing start is true. Then, for each positive integer k, the k th arrival of Process 6 occurs at time t'+(k-1)*T6.

In this example, periodic processing start of the 3 rd ptw is false. So in the first major time frame, it is not possible for periodic processing of Partition 1 to begin when this ptw starts. But even if periodic processing start for this ptw would be true, then in the scenario above, Process 6 would still not arrive in the beginning of this ptw; the reason is that the switch to normal mode has not yet happened. Also, note that the notion of mode in ARINC 653 applies to a partition; this is different from the notion of mode in some works in schedulability analysis [20,21] in which mode applies to the entire system. These interpretations are stated in the table below. They depend on which time intervals that guaranteed service applies to.

div.p: All intervals.

Formal statement of meaning: For each partition p, for each time interval of length equal to the period of p, it holds that the amount of processing time allocated to p is greater than or equal to the duration of p.

Formal statement of meaning: For each partition p, there exists an instant tp, for each time interval of length equal to the period of p such that the start time of the interval differs from tp by an integer multiple of the period of p, it holds that the amount of processing time allocated to p is greater than or equal to the duration of p.
Two partitions may have different periods; e.g., one may let the period of Partition 1 be half of the period of Partition 2 because Partition 1 has more frequent ptws.
The ARINC 653 standard does not mandate any relationship between the period of a partition and the periods of the processes in the partition. It states (page 7 in [2]), however:

Typically, the partition period is the greatest common factor of the process periods within a partition. If the process periods are harmonic, then this is the period of the process in a partition that has the shortest period. We do not make this assumption; our paper is more general.

Since a partition can have many processes, it is necessary to have a rule to determine which process in a partition should be selected for execution at run-time. ARINC 653 uses fixedpriority preemptive scheduling meaning that each process is assigned, before run-time, a priority which is a number and at run-time whenever there is a need to select one process for execution (i.e., there is more than one process eligible for execution) the one with the highest priority among the eligible processes is selected for execution. The notion of priority is represented in different ways in different technologies. In some technologies (e.g., CAN bus) a low number means that a message has high priority. But in other technologies (many operating systems), a high priority of a process is represented by a high number. div.head: B. Multicore
div.p: A multicore is a computer with many processors implemented on a single chip. Each of these processors is called a processor core. Hence, the computer can execute many processes simultaneously. We are interested in multicores that share memory because these are common in practice and these are the focus of ARINC 653. Typically, these multicores have a shared physical address space and there are various resources in the memory system (cache memories that store frequently accessed data items; write back buffers that store data that a program has written to but where the write has not yet taken effect in the main memory; hardware prefetch units that speculatively fetch data in anticipation of the data that a program needs to access).

An important consequence of these shared resources in the memory system is that they can cause inter-core interference; that is, the execution of one process on one processor core can influence the execution of another process on another processor core (typically, this influence is slowing down the execution of the other process). There are also inter-core interference that is not caused by the memory system; for example:

(i) with hyperthreading(HT)/simultaneous multithreading (SMT), two processes can be assigned to different processor cores but these two cores share hardware resources, (ii) even without HT/SMT, some processor cores have a shared floating-point unit, and (iii) the execution of one process on one processor core can increase the temperature of this processor core and also other processor cores and this can cause power/thermal-management mechanisms to "kick-in" to decrease the clock frequency of other processor cores.

The slowdown caused by inter-core interference depends on application characteristics and the processor architectures. With some applications, it has been shown that the slowdown is 2.5 times [9]. With carefully selected applications designed to stress the miss-status holding register running on x86 processors, it has been shown that the slowdown can be 103x [10]. Even more extreme experiments have shown slowdown of 300x and 1000x [11]. It is a natural question to ask: What is the worst-case slowdown in a typical application? We believe it is hard to answer because the slowdown depends on specific phasings/interleavings of memory accesses from the processes on the processor cores and there is a very large number of those interleavings.

div.head: C. Multicore ARINC 653
div.p: In recent years, ARINC 653 has been extended for multicores. The basic idea is that: (i) a partition is assigned a set of virtual processor cores, (ii) a process in the partition is assigned to a virtual core local to the partition, (iii) the partition also provides a mapping from the local virtual processor cores of the partition to physical processor cores, and (iv) at each instant, there is at most one partition active. We will assume this behavior in the rest of the paper; other ideas, however, have been considered for standardization (e.g., allowing processes to migrate between processor cores and allowing two or more partitions to active simultaneously) but we will not consider them in this paper. The reason for our choosing this is based on the following text from the ARINC 653 standard (page 5 in [2]):

div.head: Core Modules with Multiple Processor
div.p: Cores….This standard currently only defines use of multiple processes within a partition scheduled to execute concurrently on different processor cores. Definition of scheduling behaviors associated with multiple partitions scheduled to execute concurrently on different processor cores may be provided in a future revision. Fig. 3 illustrates multicore ARINC 653.

div.head: D. Different perspectives in industry and academia
div.p: We, the authors of this paper, are affiliated with a federally funded research and development center and because of this, we are in-between academia and industry. We have noticed a number of differences between the culture in academic and industry related to satisfying real-time requirements of software. We point them out here:

The academic community of real-time systems research assumes that a software system is organized as a set of concurrently executing units called tasks. A task corresponds to a process in ARINC 653. It is common to introduce a model for this; for example, a model that specifies that each task arrives periodically, whenever it arrives it needs to finish before a pre-specified deadline, and execution time (and other parameters). Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) analysis refers to obtaining an upper bound on the execution time of a task. Once the WCET of each task has been found, one proves (or disproves) the correctness of the timing of the software system as a whole. This is called schedulability analysis and it takes as input a model of the software system and outputs a result stating that all deadlines will be met or not; this relies also on a model of the resource management scheme(s) used at run-time (e.g., fixed-priority preemptive scheduling of processor cores).

In industry, we have seen different cultures in different sectors; the aerospace industry is most important for our purpose here. We have seen that in some systems, there is no specification of tasks and there is no specification of deadlines; instead, there is a notion of testing the software system in its environment and the goal is to make sure that there is as little variability as possible because if the variability is small and if the interaction with the physical world is good in a testing environment, then it is reasonable to assume that the interaction with the physical world will be good as well when the system is put into operation. ARINC 653 supports this idea of decreasing variability in timing because it has a time-triggered scheduling of ptws, and it often uses mechanisms to flush cache memories and TLBs on partition context switches so that the software in one partition is less dependent on software in another partition.

It is noteworthy that ARINC 653 also supports some of the academic perspective because ARINC 653 encourages describing the software system as a set of processes, it supports fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, and it encourages specifying processes with period and deadline. Hence, we believe bringing academic ideas to ARINC 653 is worthwhile; it will be helpful for software practitioners in aerospace.

div.head: E. Different attempts to deal with inter-core interference
div.p: The academic research community has developed operating systems mechanisms that eliminate or mitigate some inter-core interference channels. This includes (i) cache coloring [14], (ii) bank coloring [16], (iii) coordinated cache and bank coloring [16], (iv) cache locking [15], (v) TLB coloring [17], and (vi) memory bus policing [18]. Some of these (cache coloring and memory bus policing) have been implemented by RTOS vendors.

For many inter-core interference channels, there is no mechanism to eliminate it or mitigate it. Therefore, the academic community has modelled the resources and arbitration mechanism to develop analytic methods that can account for the timing effect caused by the inter-core interference channel caused by these resources (see [19] for one example). This relies on documentation of hardware. Unfortunately, such documentation is often not available, is often incorrect, and even when it is available and is correct, it is very laborious to develop such analytic methods. Many resources cannot be accounted for in this way.

Recent work [8] has developed analytic methods to account for undocumented hardware. The idea is to describe for each process, a lower bound on its execution speed as a function of co-runner processes; then take this description as input to an analytic method that can determine whether the process meets its deadline considering all possible schedules that the system can generate. These lower bounds on execution speed are obtained empirically through testing. This approach works as long as one can trust these lower bounds on execution speed but it has the drawback that it can be hard to know if the obtained estimate of the lower bound really is a lower bound. Nonetheless, despite this drawback, we believe that considering the current state-of-the-art/practice, we recommend using this approach because it fits the situation that many software practitioners are in (undocumented hardware).

CAST-32A is a guidance document for avionics; it states objectives but does not propose solutions for satisfaction of real-time requirements. ARINC 653 recognizes that inter-core interference exists but states that it does not focus on inter-core interference. Specifically, it states (page 5 in [2]):

Certification considerations, including partitioning associated with core module resources (e.g., shared cache, memory controller) shared by multiple processor cores are outside the scope of this standard.

div.head: F. Assumptions
div.p: We have already stated some assumptions that we make in this paper. In addition, we make the following assumptions: A1. We assume that processes do not self-suspend. There are primitives in ARINC 653 that are potentially blocking (operations on counting semaphores, mutexes, and message passing). We assume that these are not used. A2. We assume that processes do not request to execute non-preemptively. There is a primitive (called lock_preempt) in ARINC 653 and we assume that this is not used.

A3. We assume that the operating system uses some means to make sure that the speed of execution of one partition does not depend on execution of another partition. One way to achieve this (which is done in some operating systems) is to flush the cache and TLB after each ptw. A4. We allow for the possibility that a process in one partition executing on one processor core can experience smaller execution speed (due to inter-core interference) from another process on another processor core if the other process is in the same partition. Indeed, our schedulability analysis takes this effect into account.

A5. We assume that each process is assigned to a processor core; i.e., it does not migrate between processor cores. The rationale for this assumption is to make it compatible with safety guidance. Specifically, the EASA-AMC-20-193 guidance [12] states (in Section 2.2.1): "This AMC does not cover MCP platforms on which software applications or tasks can be dynamically reallocated to a different core (or different cores) by the operating system, a software hypervisor, or by other means." CAST-32A makes a very similar statement [13].

div.head: III. MODEL, NOTATION, AND TERMINOLOGY
div.p: To have a formal proof, we need to model a system. We will present a system model with parameters so that by assigning values to these parameters, a software practitioner obtains a model of the actual system of interest. Section A and B below provide such a system model (based on [8] adapted for ARINC 653).

div.head: A. System model
div.p: We consider a set of processes τ and a computer platform Π. Let PART denote the set of partitions. A process τi∈τ is characterized by the parameters Ti, Di, prioi, and parti with the interpretation that (i) Ti is the period of process τi; its meaning is the same as the meaning in ARINC 653 and (ii) Di is the deadline of process τi; in ARINC 653, it is called "time capacity", (iii) prioi is the priority of process τi; its meaning is the same as the one in ARINC 653; and (iv) parti is the partition to which process τi is assigned. Let Pl denote the period of partition l and let Ql denote the duration of partition l.

At run-time a process arrives periodically. Each time a process arrives, it clearly requests to execute and we call this requested execution a job. Hence a process generates a sequence of jobs. Let τi,q denote the q th job of process τi. Each job has an arrival time and a deadline. The deadline of a job of process τi is Di time units after the arrival time of this job. If a job finishes by its deadline, then we say that the job meets its deadline. The arrival time of the k th job of process τi is Ti time units after the arrival time of the k-1 th job of process τi. We assume that for each process τi it holds that Di≤Ti (this is called constrained-deadline periodic processes).

It is also necessary to describe the resource consumption of jobs and how they influence their execution speed. Previous work [8] used a model where each process is described by a set of segments. We will use this model here as well. The reason for using this description is that it allows describing different parts of a program having different sensitivities with respect to how much slowdown they experience from other programs.

Let Vi denote the set of segments of process τi. The interpretation is that the segments in Vi are ordered so that the k th segments in Vi is called vi k . Note that, a process is permitted to have just a single segment; if so |Vi |=1 and vi 1 is this single segment. A job of process τi executes its segments in order; that is, it executes segment vi 1 first; then if there is a 2 nd segment, it executes segment vi 2 ; and so on. Eventually, when the last segment of the job has finished, the job finishes. Segment vi k is described with Ci k ; the meaning is that the execution requirement of vi k is in [0, Ci k ]; that is, Ci k represents the worst-case execution requirement. Ci k influences how long it takes for segment vi k to execute but the time it takes depends on its co-runners which can be different at different times.

We introduce a speed of execution of a segment vi k at a time given a schedule. Since a schedule is given, one can identify which other segments executes at this time when vi k executes; we call these other segments co-runners. The execution speed of segment vi k given co-runners is not fixed so we describe it with a lower bound and an upper bound.

Let the lower bound on the execution speed of segment vi k given co-runners co be denoted pwi,co k and let the upper bound on the execution speed of segment vi k given co-runner co be 1. The intuition behind this notation is that pw can be thought of as progress worst case and this can be thought of as meaning lower bound on the speed of execution. In order to represent the lower bound with parameters, we introduce COi k as a set of tuples where each tuple <csi,h k , pcsi,h k > has the meaning that if vi k has the co-runner set csi,h k then pwi,co k is pcsi,h k . The segment vi k is also characterized by pdi k , meaning progress default; this provides a lower bound on the execution speed of segment vi k if such a bound is not provided by COi k for a certain co.

A segment finishes when the number of units of execution it has completed is equal to its execution requirement. The completed number of units of execution of a segment in a time interval is the integral of the speed of execution of the segment over the time interval.

Note that we have not specified how many jobs a process generates; and we have not specified the arrival times of jobs (only that they are periodic but we did not specify the time when the first job of a process arrives); we did not specify the execution requirement of a segment (only specified an upper bound on it); we did not specify the speed of execution of a segment (only a lower and upper bound on it). Therefore, there are many possible schedules that the system can generate.

We say that a system (described by a set of processes τ, a computer platform Π, and partitions PART) is schedulable if for all schedules that it can generate, for all processes, for all jobs in this schedule, the job meets its deadline. Later, we will make the notion of schedulable more precise.
We are interested in finding a condition such that if this condition is true, then the system is schedulable.

div.head: B. Notation that we will find useful
div.p: When presenting and proving the schedulability condition, we will find the following notation useful.
Let a schedule sc be an assignment for each time, for each processor core, the process and segment that executes at the time if any.

A schedule depends on the scheduler and the aforementioned parameters whose values are known before the system starts operation but it also depends on parameters whose values are determined at run-time (for each process, the number of jobs it generates, and for each job, its arrival time, and for each segment of a job, its execution requirement). Therefore, we define an assignment R as an assignment, for each process, the number of jobs it generates, and for each job, its arrival time, and for each segment of a job, its execution requirement. Let AiD,qD(R) denote the arrival time of τi,q for the assignment R.

We use the notion of legal assignment to express that the assignment respects our system model. Formally, we say that an assignment R is legal with respect to the set of processes τ if for each process τi∈τ, it holds that:
1. for each job of τi such that the job is not the first job of τi, the arrival time of the job is Ti time units after the arrival time of the previous job of process τi.

2. for each job of τi, for each segment vi k of this job, the execution requirement is in [0,Ci k ] Let a progress function pa be a mapping from a task, a job index, a segment index, a co-runner set, and a time to a real number (which indicates speed of execution).

We say that a progress function pa is legal for a set of processes τ and a computer platform Π if it respects that the execution speed is at most 1 and at least pw as defined earlier and also that pa is Lebesgue integrable over time.

We say that a system (described by a set of processes τ, a computer platform Π, and partitions PART) is schedulable if for each progress function, assignment, and schedule such that the progress function is legal, the assignment is legal, and the schedule can be generated from the progress function and the assignment, it holds that all deadlines in the schedule are met.

Recall that legal makes a claim over all jobs. Later in a proof, we will find it instrumental to use another notion that we call legalrelax which takes as input a specific task index i and a specific job index q. The meaning of legalrelax is very similar to legal; it differs only in that with legalrelax, it holds that if q≥2, then the job τi,q must arrive after the finishing time of job τi,q-1 but we do not require that the arrival time of τi,q is Ti time units after τi,q-1. Note that legalrelax is more permissive than legal and it allows a process to have a single job that is not periodic.

div.head: IV. NEW SCHEDULABILITY TEST
div.p: Section A presents a proof of a condition that is true for a system that misses a deadline. In Section B, we will turn this into a condition for proving that deadlines are met. This condition depends on a function called sbfI (meaning supply bound function) that depends on the interpretation I of period and duration of a partition. Therefore, Section C presents this function for I=0 (which means that sbfI is computed directly from the module schedule, i.e., not from period and duration); Section D presents this function for I≥1.

div.head: A. Unschedulable
div.p: Let us consider a system with a computer platform Π with a set of processes τ, and a set of partitions PART. Suppose that the system is unschedulable. Then, there is an assignment R, a progress function pa, and a schedule sc such that the following conditions are true:

1. R is legal with respect to the set of processes τ 2. pa is legal for a set of processes τ and a computer platform Π 3. sc is a schedule that can be generated by the system for the assignment R and the progress function pa 4. in the schedule sc there is a deadline miss For sc, find the earliest time when a deadline is missed. There is at least one job whose deadline is missed at this time.
Choose one such job and call it τiD,qD. (on any processor, not just prociD) that arrive after AiD,qD(R)+t. Hence, for the chosen t∈[0,DiD], it holds that:

5. The job τiD,qD has not finished at time AiD,qD(R)+t.

div.head: No job arrives after AiD,qD(R)+t
div.p: We will now discuss legality of the assignment R. We claim that when no deadline miss occurs before AiD,qD(R) + t, for R, sc, iD, qD, it holds that: R is legal with respect to τ ⇒ R is legalrelax with respect to sc, iD, qD, τ

This claim can be proven as follows: assume that the lhs of the above is true. If qD = 1, then there is no preceding job of τiD,qD and hence from the definition of legalrelax this implies that the rhs of the above claim is true. Let us now discuss the case that qD ≥ 2. Since the lhs of the above claim is true and no deadline miss occurs before AiD,qD(R) + t, it follows that τiD,qD-1 meets its deadline. Since we have constrained-deadline periodic tasks, it follows that the finishing time of τiD,qD-1 is less than or equal to AiD,qD(R) and then it follows that an assignment that is legal is also legalrelax. This implies that the rhs of the above claim is true.
Applying the above claim yields:
1. R is legalrelax with respect to sc, iD, qD, and the set of processes τ 2. pa is legal for a set of processes τ and a computer platform Π
3. sc is a schedule that can be generated by the system for the assignment R and the progress function pa 4. No deadline miss occurs before AiD,qD(R)+t.
5. The job τiD,qD has not finished at time AiD,qD(R)+t.
